**CFPB confirmation hearing puts open banking fees and AI oversight in focus**

*Brian Johnson's Senate hearing to lead the CFPB is testing whether the bureau's rewritten open banking rule, with its controversial data fees for fintechs, will survive political scrutiny.*

The Senate Banking Committee held a confirmation hearing on July 22 for Brian Johnson, nominated to serve as permanent director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Open banking data fees, a centrepiece of the bureau's revised rule published in late June under acting director Russell Vought, featured prominently in questioning.

The revised rule narrowed the scope of data banks must share and introduced fees that fintechs would pay to access consumer information, a significant departure from the original 2024 rule that prohibited such charges. Industry trade groups representing credit unions have pressed for a voice in shaping how the final framework works in practice, while fintech lobbies have argued the fee structure violates the Trump administration's own executive order on reducing regulatory costs.

Johnson's confirmation will determine whether the CFPB pursues this fee-based model or revisits it. For European observers, the US approach is diverging sharply from the EU and UK frameworks, where API access costs have been a persistent friction point but outright data fees on third-party providers remain outside the regulatory conversation.

*Sources: [CFPB director nomination hearing 2026: Live coverage](https://www.americanbanker.com/live-blog/cfpb-director-nomination-hearing-2026-live-coverage) — American Banker | [CONSUMER FINANCIAL PROTECTION BUREAU—DCUC wants a voice at CFPB ...](https://www.vitallaw.com/news/consumer-financial-protection-bureau-dcuc-wants-a-voice-at-cfpb-confirmation-hearing/blw01273c6e86bc2c4466b632a05d4644320b) — VitalLaw.com*

**FCA selects Anthropic for second phase of its AI regulatory sandbox**

*The UK regulator's decision to partner with Anthropic signals a shift from broad AI policy statements to hands-on testing, with implications for how AI is supervised in payments and financial services.*

The Financial Conduct Authority is partnering with Anthropic, the US AI firm behind the Claude model, for the second phase of its AI sandbox. The programme is designed to let the regulator test how AI tools function in supervised financial services settings before writing formal rules.

The FCA published its AI review earlier in July, placing open finance and agentic payments squarely within scope. Selecting Anthropic — rather than a European AI developer — as the sandbox partner suggests the regulator is prioritising capability over provenance in its testing work. The choice also reflects the reality that the most advanced large language models used in financial services originate outside Europe.

For payments firms exploring agentic commerce and AI-driven processes, the sandbox's findings will shape what the FCA considers acceptable use. The second phase is expected to examine how AI interacts with regulated activities such as payment initiation, risk assessment and customer communications.

*Sources: [LATEST: FCA taps Anthropic for AI sandbox second phase](https://www.amlintelligence.com/2026/07/fca-taps-anthropic-for-ai-sandbox-second-phase/) — AML Intelligence*

**Major hotel chains launch open banking debit cards for UK travellers**

*Hilton, Marriott and IHG have each launched UK debit cards built on open banking rails, using Currensea's infrastructure to offer real-time exchange rates and loyalty integration at the point of spend.*

Three of the world's largest hotel groups — Hilton, Marriott and IHG — have launched co-branded debit cards in the UK that use open banking connections to customers' existing bank accounts rather than requiring a separate prepaid balance or credit facility. The cards are built on infrastructure from Currensea, a UK fintech that links directly to users' current accounts.

The model bypasses traditional card issuance entirely. Customers connect their bank account via open banking, and the Currensea-powered card draws funds in real time, offering foreign exchange rates as low as 0.5% on the top-tier product. Loyalty points accrue directly on spending, creating a proposition that competes with travel credit cards from the major banks.

The convergence of three competing hotel brands on the same open banking model is notable not for the individual launches but for what it reveals about where embedded finance is finding traction. Travel spending — high-value, cross-border, loyalty-driven — is proving a natural fit for open banking distribution beyond the pure fintech segment.

*Sources: [Hilton, Marriott, and IHG Have All Launched UK Debit Cards. Here's Why.](https://skift.com/2026/07/22/hilton-marriott-and-ihg-have-all-launched-uk-debit-cards-heres-why/) — Skift*

**Georgia's central bank partners with Bank of Korea on open finance framework**

*The National Bank of Georgia is working with South Korean counterparts to design an open finance ecosystem, extending a bilateral relationship that already produced the country's lari-backed stablecoin initiative.*

The National Bank of Georgia and the Bank of Korea have signed a bilateral agreement under which Korean experts will help design an open finance framework for Georgia. The collaboration falls within the Knowledge Partnership Program, a longer-standing arrangement between the two institutions.

Georgia has been building its digital financial infrastructure at an unusual pace for its size. The country launched a lari-backed stablecoin with Tether in May, and the central bank is now looking to establish the data-sharing rules and technical standards needed for an open finance ecosystem. South Korea's own open banking system, which has seen rapid consumer adoption since its 2019 launch, provides a relatively mature model to draw from.

The partnership illustrates how open finance frameworks are spreading through bilateral technical cooperation rather than solely through EU or UK regulatory influence. For European providers, Georgia's emerging infrastructure represents both a potential market and a test of whether open finance models can be adapted outside the EU's regulatory perimeter.

*Sources: [NBG, Bank of Korea sign bilateral agreement within Knowledge Partnership Program](https://1tv.ge/lang/en/news/nbg-bank-of-korea-sign-bilateral-agreement-within-knowledge-partnership-program/) — 1TV*
